---
title: "3. Exponential Population"
subtitle: "Strong right skew, and a direct test of the 'n = 30' rule"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/clt_helpers.R")
rate <- 1
gen_exp <- function(k) rexp(k, rate = rate)
```

## What population am I sampling from?

Exponential with rate $\lambda = 1$, generated with `rexp()`. It's continuous, can't go below 0, and has a long **right tail**. It's the kind of shape you see for waiting times or wait-until-failure times.

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig-height: 4
plot_population(gen_exp, "Population: Exponential(rate = 1)", xlim = c(0, 8))
curve(dexp(x, rate), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

| Quantity | Theoretical value |
|---|---|
| Mean $\mu = 1/\lambda$ | 1 |
| SD $\sigma = 1/\lambda$ | 1 |
| Skewness | 2 |
| Excess kurtosis | 6 |
| $SE(\bar X)$ | $1/\sqrt{n}$ |

```{r}
mu <- 1 / rate; sigma <- 1 / rate; g1 <- 2; g2 <- 6
```

## What did I expect?

This is the case where I think $n = 30$ will **not** be enough. The skewness of $\bar X$ is $2/\sqrt{n}$, so at $n = 30$ it's still $2/\sqrt{30} \approx `r round(2/sqrt(30), 2)`$, which is above my 0.25 cutoff. Solving $2/\sqrt n < 0.25$:

```{r}
predicted_n(g1, g2)
```

My prediction: skewness is the bottleneck, and the answer lands somewhere around $n = 64$.

## Which sample sizes did I investigate?

The standard grid from 1 to 500, with $B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")`$ repetitions. The grid is dense between 30 and 100 (30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100), which is exactly where I expected the cutoff to be, so I can pin it down.

## Simulation

```{r}
#| label: simulate
sweep  <- run_sweep(function(n) simulate_means(gen_exp, n, B), mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
tab    <- sweep$table
n_star <- chosen_n(tab)
show_table(tab)
```

```{r}
#| label: pictures
#| fig-height: 12
plot_sampling(sweep, c(1, 5, 30, n_star), mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
```

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot_convergence(tab)
```

I also compared the simulated skewness to the theory curve $2/\sqrt n$:

```{r}
#| label: skew-vs-theory
#| fig-height: 4
plot(tab$n, tab$skewness, log = "x", pch = 19,
     xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "Skewness of sample means",
     main = "Simulated skewness vs. theory 2/sqrt(n)")
curve(2 / sqrt(x), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(h = skew_cut, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
legend("topright", c("Simulated", "Theory 2/sqrt(n)", "My cutoff"),
       col = c("black", "firebrick", "gray40"), pch = c(19, NA, NA),
       lty = c(NA, 1, 2), bty = "n")
```

## Theory vs. simulation

- **Mean:** every simulated mean is within `r round(max(abs(tab$sim_mean - mu)), 3)` of 1.
- **Standard error:** simulated SE / $(1/\sqrt n)$ ranged from `r round(min(tab$se_ratio), 3)` to `r round(max(tab$se_ratio), 3)`. So the SE formula works at every $n$, even $n = 1$ where the shape is nowhere near normal. **The formula for the SE being right does not mean the shape is normal.** Those are two different questions.
- **Shape:** the simulated skewness follows $2/\sqrt n$ really closely.

At $n = 30$ specifically:

```{r}
knitr::kable(signif(tab[tab$n == 30, c("n", "skewness", "ex_kurt", "qq_cor", "shapiro_p")], 3))
```

## When is it approximately normal?

$$
\boxed{n = `r n_star`}
$$

That's very close to my prediction of 64. At $n = `r n_star`$ the skewness drops to `r round(tab$skewness[tab$n == n_star], 3)` and the Q-Q correlation reaches `r round(tab$qq_cor[tab$n == n_star], 4)`. Kurtosis was never the bottleneck: it passed my cutoff early, just like theory said. You can still see a slight upward bend at the right end of the Q-Q plot at $n = 30$, which is the leftover right skew.

## Reproducibility experiment

The assignment asks what happens with a different seed. I reran the exact same sweep, but with seeds based on 1234 instead of my ID:

```{r}
#| label: reproducibility
sweep_alt <- run_sweep(function(n) simulate_means(gen_exp, n, B, seed = 1234 + n),
                       mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
tab_alt <- sweep_alt$table
n_star_alt <- chosen_n(tab_alt)

compare <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  skew_my_seed  = round(tab$skewness, 3),
  skew_alt_seed = round(tab_alt$skewness, 3),
  pass_my_seed  = tab$normal_enough,
  pass_alt_seed = tab_alt$normal_enough
)
knitr::kable(compare[compare$n >= 30 & compare$n <= 150, ], row.names = FALSE)
```

- **Did the exact results change?** Yes. Every number changes a little, because they're different random draws.
- **Did my conclusion change?** With my seed the answer is $n = `r n_star`$ and with the other seed it's $n = `r n_star_alt`$. `r if (n_star == n_star_alt) "Same answer." else "Close, but not identical, because near the cutoff the skewness is only slightly above or below 0.25, so noise can tip it one way or the other."` The big conclusion (somewhere around 60 to 80, definitely not 30) doesn't change.

What this tells me about Monte Carlo: the seed makes the *exact* numbers reproducible, but the *conclusion* should be robust to the seed. If changing the seed flipped my conclusion completely, it would mean $B$ is too small or my cutoff is right on the edge of the noise.

## What surprised me?

How well the theory predicted the simulation. I expected "about 60-ish" and the simulated skewness sat right on top of the $2/\sqrt n$ curve. I was also surprised that the SE formula was accurate at $n = 1$, when the histogram of means is literally just the exponential distribution. It made it clear that the CLT is a statement about **shape**, not about the mean or the SE.

```{r}
#| label: save
save_results("Exponential", tab, n_star,
             "Skewness 2/sqrt(n) is the bottleneck; n = 30 is not enough")
```
